Chapter 18: Part Eighteen: The Market
Chapter Summary

Distantly, you wished you could stay in this moment forever. You wanted to stay
suspended in the moment between his confession and when he would dance away again,
forbidding himself from straying too close. If only you could live like this for eternity,
you thought, hanging in this moment where the cool evening breeze tickled your warm
cheeks and the shower of petals fell between the two of you. Maybe then you could take
a step closer, try to see the eyes beneath Din's helmet as they gazed back into you.

Chapter Notes

Recommended listening for courtyard scene: "Princess Liea's theme"

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Raider's Cove was just as busy as it had been the first time you, Mando, and the child had
arrived on the planet. The bustling downtown marketplace hummed with life, bodies pushing
past each other on narrow streets and platforms. Being in such a crowd only worsened the
humid thick air of the lowlands, which was a far cry from the cooler elevated heights of the
Rishi village. The cacophony of the urban jungle neared deafening at times. Merchants
loudly hawked their wares and travelers pushed through the throng of chattering residents.
Yet the atmosphere was lively, friendly as neighbors and vendors talked over the noisy crowd
with wide smiles and good-natured haggling.

You had been the one to convince Mando to take a trip into town and reluctantly, he had
agreed. While you had been enthusiastic at a day out shopping, your excitement had been
dulled by your companion’s tense silence beside you. The presence of so many eyes glancing
at the stranger with the beskar cuirass and small green child unsettled him, you knew. It was
the way his hands remained closed at his sides, gait controlled and body stiff as you traversed
the marketplace. If the situation weren’t dire you would have regretted dragging him beyond
the secluded Rishii village.

At the same time, you could only stand so many days of walking around in borrowed and
bloodied clothes. You only had the clothes on your back during your escape from Kaddak and
had somehow managed to keep them decently clean during your travels so far. However now
that they had been shredded and stained whilst defending the child and the Razorcrest, trying
to upkeep that habit was impossible. Plus, you could only borrow the spare shirt you had
found on the ship for so long. You assumed it was Mando's, and if your other clothes weren’t
in such bad shape you would have felt a little embarrassed to be using it for so long.



Even now your shirt, which clung to your sweaty form like a second skin, bore the damage
from your struggle a week prior. You had opted to leave Mando's freshly laundered shirt on
the Razorcrest, hesitantly swapping it for the sliced shirt and overalls you had worn before.
Your only saving grace preventing you from being exposed was a poncho, lent to you by one
of the village girls, which hid the scarlet stain and ripped fabric from wandering eyes.

You carried the child in your arms tucked against the woven material of the poncho and could
see his wide brown gaze darting to take in the colorful marketplace with dyed fabrics and
exotic wares. Fruits you had never seen before decorated the food stands, and as you walked
you could smell a mouthwatering delicacy from one of the creaky wooden walkways above
you. A glance upward showed a spiral of cooking smoke floating up into the lilac-colored
sky. Colorfully dyed fabrics hung from clotheslines above the street, wavering gently in the
salty ocean breeze.

It was familiar, in some ways, to be back in busy streets. Rishi was comparably different from
the dry, cracked air of Kaddak. Where your home planet had mud structures with fissured
walls from the blazing heat of the sun and a forever orange tint on the horizon, Rishi spoke in
its language of cobbled together buildings, wooden walkways, and creeping foliage. Yet the
thrumming heartbeat of the city echoed within you as a familiar friend, one you had known
all your life.

Mando had remained glued to your side, commanding space in the packed streets and
alleyways you navigated. Every time that you had to force your way through a group of
people or step around a vendor with arms full of goods Mando had guided you around and
through the throng. When you stopped for directions, it was Mando who spoke in a low but
authoritative tone. Idling groups parted upon seeing his black visor lock onto them, shuffling
respectfully out of the way for you three to pass. More than once Mando had tucked you into
his side with a careful grip, maneuvering you away from a particularly rough looking cluster
of travelers or a shady individual.

Weeks ago, you would have flinched at his gentle hand on your shoulder or at the small of
your back. Yet after all this time alongside him, his simple gesture was reassuring, protective
even. You couldn't help but feel as if you had your own personal bodyguard, vigilant and
stern yet treating you as if you were made of glass. A small huff of laughter left you, earning
a curious 'patu' from the toddler in your arms. You smiled down at him and let a finger trace
his long green ears, to which he gave you a toothy smile.

Then you turned your attention to the Mando beside you, watching him scan the marketplace
with a hawk-like gaze, investigating for threats and possible dangers that lurked in the
darkened alleyways of the market. You could tell from the stiffened set of his shoulders, the
way his hands were clenched at his sides, that he was anxious at being surrounded by this
many people. You wished you could pull him aside, try to reassure him and watch his body
language relax at the sound of your voice.

Din, he said his name was. The sound was warm, like a friend. Yet on your tongue it tasted
foreign, forbidden. He had confessed it in the moments where you two sat a breath away
from each other, wounds open and gazes wide at each other's vulnerability. He hadn't insisted
you call him as much since then, and you felt almost as if you did not deserve this secret title



which he had offered to you. Yet alone in your bunk at night, hidden in the dark recesses of
the village hut on the straw mattress, you let the sound ripple over your tongue in secret.

Since that moment aboard the Razorcrest he had changed. You couldn't decipher why, but
Din’s behavior had shifted since that morning. At times he was soft, closing the distance
between you in ways you had not expected. He offered to help reach shelves you couldn't,
letting a hand brush on your shoulder to signal he was passing you in the cargo hold. He sat
with you in the evenings as the child fell asleep in your arms, beskar helmet dancing with the
shadows of the fire. He let himself relax, let his voice soften as he spoke to you over the
sound of the child's gentle snores.

Then, as if remembering something, he would leave just as quickly as he had come, once
again creating the wall he had constructed between you. You would get a brief good night, a
farewell before he vanished into the ship. You wished you could understand, could fathom his
strange contradictory actions. He seemed at war with himself over something you couldn't
see nor comprehend.

"Here." Din spoke, interjecting himself between your thoughts. Abruptly he nodded towards
an empty alleyway leading to a shaded shop away from the busy street. Before you could
blink he was once again leading you carefully by the elbow away from the main street and
towards the smaller pathway. You had to squeeze after him, the both of you sidestepping
through the alleyway to where it opened up again at the end. Stepping out of the shadows
revealed a small open space between the ruck shack buildings, allowing the afternoon
sunlight to stream through and illuminate you three.

A curtained doorway sat in the side of a ruck shack metal building, its tin roof reflecting the
tropical sun above. You gave Mando a cursory glance, unsure of his particular choice in
venue. Yet you allowed yourself to be directed forward, walking in front of Mando as he
slunk into the shop behind you.

As you pushed past the threadbare curtain into the shop, you could see only a simple
worktable, a number of materials scattered about, and an archway to a backroom that
revealed a number of crates, boxes, and containers. The counter itself was tended by a slender
Nautolan girl who was leaning over a holopad. Her garments differed from the loose, colorful
fabrics of the native residents in the market before. Instead, she looked almost as if she had
come from the mid-rim, with her collared shirt and fitted pocketed pants. As you three
crowded into the small shop space she stood, letting her eyes linger over Mando's shiny
beskar armor.

"What can I get you for?" She asked bluntly, tucking a stylus into a pocket brimming with
tools. Her voice had a slow drawl to it, and it reminded you of a traveler you had spoken to
once who said he hailed from Corellia. "Armor maintenance?"

You stepped forward to speak, but Din interjected before you could.

"Need a couple sets of clothes, a flight suit, and a plastoid armor chest piece." He rattled off
in his typical low modulated tone. Before you could add anything he turned to you, taking the
green toddler from your arms, and instead pressing a small bag of credits into your palm. You
gaped at the weight, feeling the credits within sink into your hands.



"Wait, Mando." You interjected hurriedly. "This is so much, where-"

"It was the bounty for the Clawdite." He murmured, lowering his voice so the shopkeeper
couldn't hear. "It's yours."

You shook your head almost frantically, brow furrowing. You couldn’t accept this. You had
never made this much at once during all your years as a mechanic. "B-but you were the one
who-"

"It wasn't my blaster bolt that killed them." Din insisted, ignoring the reach of the child in his
arms trying the grasp the mysterious sachet in your hands. In the partial sunlight of the
doorway his shadow fell over you. His visored gaze locked onto yours, and you knew
beneath it he was giving you a stern yet kind stare.

"It's yours." He insisted again, and you remembered to close your gaping mouth before
nodding. You felt a flush rise to your face, one that you couldn't attribute to the humid
atmosphere.

"Don't get cheated." He warned in a murmur, bending so the modulator on his helmet brushed
up against your hair. You felt your heart thump at how suddenly close he was. "Find me
outside when you're done."

You nodded, watching as he turned and pushed the curtain closed behind him. He paused
outside, armor glinting with the sunlight. He turned halfway back towards you, nodding once
before vanishing back into the alleyway from which you had both come.

Turning to the Nautolan behind the counter, you offered her a small smile. In return she
raised an eyebrow at you, curious but offering no questions pertaining to you or your two odd
travel companions. After a beat she sighed and waved you behind the counter.

"Let's get started then, shall we?"

----

It took at least a few hours, but eventually you had assembled enough clothes to ensure you
wouldn't have to borrow any other shirts from Mando's wardrobe.

You had opted for several soft but sturdy collared shirts, letting the top buttons open for
freedom of movement and comfortability. You admired the shopkeeper's fitted workpants,
choosing two similar pairs for yourself as well. Added to that was a tool belt, a holster for
your blaster, and a pocketed vest.

You hadn't originally felt the need to purchase a lightweight chest plate as well, but Din's
mention of it combined with the memory of being held at gunpoint prompted you to do so. It
wasn't nearly as heavy as the beskar you had helped him get out of to treat his wounds, but
the weight of it against your torso was surprisingly sturdy, if not a tad cumbersome. It
wouldn’t hold up being held at point blank, but it provided a safeguard against any long-
range fire. You likely wouldn’t have to wear it all if you simply stayed in the Razorcrest next



time Din went on a hunt. Still, having something to keep you safe was likely a sound
investment.

Instead of a flight suit you picked out a pair of replacement overalls, gladly discarding your
ripped ones in a disposal bin. All of that, combined with a liberal supply of socks and
undergarments, proved to be quite the shopping haul. Relying on your bartering skills honed
by the streets of Kaddak, you managed to talk the shopkeeper down by a small number of
credits and to toss in an extra pair of boots and work gloves. Altogether it was quite the
wardrobe, enough so that you slid the shopkeeper a few extra credits in exchange for the
package to be delivered to the dock with the Razorcrest.

The sun was shifting towards the horizon by the time you pushed past the curtain and into the
outdoor alcove. Now dressed in fresh clothes, you could feel yourself ease without the burden
of self-consciousness on you. Still, your eyes anxiously scanned for Din and the child. Upon
finding yourself alone, you scooted through the alleyway back towards the main street.

The crowd had thinned since your original arrival, yet there remained a number of vendors
and wandering customers along the through-way. Even here, you didn't see Mando or the
child. Yet you had a feeling they were close by. Mando wouldn't wander far without coming
to tell you first. If you gave him time, eventually he would come find you.

So instead, you chose to browse the stands and tents available, eyes curiously roaming over
the various foreign produce and masterfully woven baskets. You chatted good-naturedly with
the shopkeepers, asking questions about their merchandise. They happily explained which
food was what, how you would prepare it, and the parts to stay away from. In the end you
were carrying a small collection of vegetables and fruit you had never tried before, figuring
that even if you didn't like them, that the kid in your care would down them without a second
thought with his voracious appetite.

Munching on a large, tart flavored berry, you found yourself pausing at a small tent near the
edge of the market. Instead of the small assortment of produce, your eyes were drawn to the
collection of carved wooden and stone tokens displayed on a decorated tapestry. Before you
could inquire, a young man peeked his head over the display, hair a shock of bright red
contrasted to his dark chocolate complexion.

"They're worry stones!" He supplied enthusiastically, vanishing once again before pivoting
his wheelchair out from behind the booth. "I make them!"

You stepped back to allow him space to maneuver to the display. In his lap lay a small cloth
with carving tools as he likely worked on another one of the trinkets. You offered the boy a
smile as he picked up one in his grip.

"You carry it around for good luck, and the texture helps ground you if you are anxious." He
explained, turning the stone so its color reflected the late sunlight. To demonstrate he ran his
finger along the grooved spine of a smoothly polished stone, letting the scrape of his nails
against the indents speak for itself. Turning, he offered it to you.

Hesitantly, you accepted, letting the worn pads of your fingers trace over the smooth
underbelly of the stone and feel the grooved ridges on top. It was strangely calming, and the



stone itself was beautiful. You didn’t find yourself particularly wanting for the trinket, despite
its masterful craftsmanship.

An odd thought occurred to you, and soon you were fishing around for the credit satchel in
your pocket.

"Just one, please." You told him, depositing three credits into his hand in return for the stone.
"Thank you."

The vendor nodded, grinning broadly at the transaction before you waved a friendly goodbye
and walked off. In one hand you traced the spine of the stone once more, listening to the
sound before tucking it into your pocket.

The afternoon light had begun to fade towards evening now as you strolled towards the far
end of the market. Still not having spotted Din and the child, you decided to begin wandering
back towards the hangar where the Razorcrest was docked. If all else failed, Din would check
to make sure you were there by nightfall.

Somewhere above you, up in the buildings that housed the vendors and their families, music
began to play. It wasn't particularly good, merely someone plucking chords on an instrument
as they practiced. Still, the sound combined with the slow-paced market stalls closing for the
day, the idle chatter of passerby and the sound of water running under the pathways allowed
an almost foreign tranquility to fall over you. It was different than the breezy and warm
atmosphere of the Rishi village. Instead, it sang in a faint voice alongside the thrum of the
city, harmonizing in an urban lullaby. For a moment, it felt like home.

It almost covered up the strange robotic garble that met your ears as you rounded a corner.
You looked up curiously, trying to pinpoint the odd sound. You could hear the sound float
over you accompanied by a low hum. To your ears it sounded like a droid, not that you had
seen any floating around the marketplace. Plus, the sound was unfamiliar, the garbled tone
sounding for a moment like radio code. Yet as you listened the sound faded beyond the tin
roofs above you.

"Found you."

You practically leapt out of your skin at the sudden voice behind you, dropping the pear in
your hand in the process. You wheeled around to face the owner, relaxing instantly upon
realizing who had snuck up on you.

"Mando." You breathed, the sharp inhale you had taken exiting as a relieved whoosh of air.
"You scared the kriff out of me."

Mando didn't answer. For a moment it seemed like he was going to speak, then stopped
himself. He stood a few steps away from you, helmeted gaze tracing your form from the
bottom up. You shifted a little under his stare, uncertain at his sudden scrutiny. When his gaze
reached your face he stopped, stiffening almost imperceptibly.

He cleared his throat, shifting his weight from one foot to the other before offering: "You
look...better."



You blinked, unprepared for what you guessed was a compliment from the hunter. Dumbly,
you looked down at yourself to realize he had noticed your change of clothes into something
more suitable and comfortable. At your feet stood the child, having taken the pear that had
fallen from your grip. He nibbled on it experimentally, making a small face of happiness
before munching enthusiastically.

"Oh." You spoke, voice soft in reply as you struggled to summon a response past your
flummoxed brain. "I- uh, thank you."

Din didn't move, eyes still lingering on your figure. You felt yourself warm under his gaze,
not entirely uncomfortable with the sudden attention.

Then, as your brain caught up, you remembered the weight in your pocket.

"Oh!" You gasped, hand fishing for the item hidden within your vest. "I- I um, I got you
something."

With one arm still full of produce, you used the other to offer Din the small carved stone you
had purchased, belated realizing that the color was not unlike that of the soft calm twilight
following the stunning Rishi sunsets.

Din merely stared at it, head bent to his chest to examine the strange object.

"What is this?" He asked flatly, and you tried to ignore the small sense of deflation at his
tone.

"It's a worry stone." You supplied. "You carry it for good luck. The vendor said when you
touch it, it absorbs your worries from you."

Hesitantly, Mando raised a gloved hand to pick up the stone from your palm. He proceeded to
raise it above him, holding it close to his visor so he could examine the translucent soft
purple coloring. The yellow lamplights of the market reflected in the gaze of his visor. Yet
despite his interest you felt an uncertain doubt gnaw at you.

"I-it's dumb." You added quickly, self-consciously. "I just saw it and I know you're nervous
because of the bounties on our heads and thought maybe- I don't know. You can just toss it if
you want-"

"Thank you."

You blinked, feeling your cheeks flush warmly. "What?"

"Thank you." Din repeated, lowering his gaze to look at you once more. "It...It's nice."

It took a moment for your brain to catch up.

Ah, you thought. There it was again, that soft heartfelt tone he only ever used with you.
Every time he spoke to you in that voice you could feel an odd lightness in your chest, lifting
you up and stealing the breath from your body.



Din regarded you in your silence, stance slack and shoulders low.

"I…guess we should head back." You offered at last, turning on your heel in the direction of
the docks. "It's getting late."

Yet when Din didn't follow you paused, casting a glance over your shoulder. The
Mandalorian looked after you, shifting his weight from one foot to the other once more. The
child at his feet gazed up at him curiously, joining your expectant gaze.

"Wait." He said at last, voice sounding oddly strained. "There's...something I want to show
you."

You tilted your head curiously, blinking at him. Yet Din didn't offer any further explanation,
merely bending to scoop the toddler at his feet into his hold. He balanced the little one in one
arm, cradling him against the beskar plating of his chest piece. The child gazed at the hunter
with a mouthful of fruit, holding the pear tight in his three-clawed grip.

"This way." Din spoke, turning without further explanation. You gazed after him silently,
confused for a moment before deciding to follow.

Din led you away from the main street, up a rope ladder ramp towards the upper levels of the
market. He paused at the top, making sure you weren't struggling to climb before moving on.
From here you could see the market street in full, nearly empty now compared to the bustle
of this morning. You let your eyes linger for a few more moments before padding behind Din
up and further into the housing sector.

You could hear families chatting now, and with every turn you could smell a different meal
being prepared with delicious spices and exotic seasoning. Longingly, you wished you had
bought some decent ingredients to try your hand at preparing a meal for you three instead of
relying on the food from the grateful Rishii villagers.

Eventually you followed Din into a narrow side street, more of an alleyway than and actual
path. The light from the street lanterns began to fade, casting twilight shadows over both your
forms.

You glanced at the Mando in front of you, trying to adjust your eyes to the darkness. There
you found a small face gazing back at you, partially hidden behind a rapidly diminishing
pear. The child peeked over Din's shoulder, long green ears sticking out in either direction.
You couldn't help but smile to yourself at how such a merciless mercenary held the child in
his arms with such delicate care.

Up ahead you blinked at a bright lantern illuminating the spot where the alleyway opened up
once more. Din's form stepped beyond the hidden path, making way for you to exit into what
looked to be a small courtyard between houses.

It was the smell you noticed first, floral yet delicately sweet. It wafted over your senses
alongside the humid, salty air of the beaches beyond the market. You filled your lungs with it,
relishing how you could practically taste in on your tongue. As you stepped into the
courtyard, you were greeted by the sound of flowing water and soft, tinkling wind chimes. A



small fountain sat to your left beside one of the entryways, piled high with baskets on the
edge of a small pool. Yet it wasn't the fountain that drew your attention, but the foliage that
draped over the stone and dipped its roots into the water like a slender touch into the ocean.

Thousands of tiny, delicate white flowers decorated the small space, weaving themselves into
a cream-colored tapestry over the wooden walls and metal exteriors of the courtyard. They
hung as a curtain, climbing ever higher up towards the roofs and balconies of the small space.
In the warm evening breeze, a small shower of white petals floated down from the heavens.
They rested atop the surface of the fountain’s pool like tiny boats adrift at sea. With a
delighted smile you reached your hand out, watching the small petals fall against your open
palm and tickling the skin there. To you it almost felt like a soft, whispered blessing from
above. One of peace and serenity.

"It's beautiful." You breathed, eyes twinkling in the warm colored light of the single lamp
illuminating the dusk dimmed courtyard. You took a step closer, gingerly lifting a handful of
the blooms to your nose and inhaling deeply. "They almost smell like honey.”

You turned to cast a glance at Din and paused upon seeing the way his entire body had
relaxed. His free hand lay slack at his side, the arm he was using the carry the child holding
on with a loose grip. The silver helmet on his head tilted gently, observing you in an almost
reverent silence. It made you catch your breath for a moment. You could not think of a time
you had seen Din so calm, so at peace.

"I hoped you would like it." He murmured, voice hinting a carefully concealed tenderness.
"It...made me think of you."

You raised a sly eyebrow at him, mouth quirking into a smirk despite the rapid flutter of your
heartbeat inside your chest. "Think of me?" You asked curiously. "As in delicate or
something?"

"No." And the sudden sharp cut of his tone surprised you. Yet his voice didn't raise,
hardening like steel for the briefest of moments as if he was almost offended by your
suggestion.

Din paused for what seemed like a long time, hand clenching and unclenching at his side. In
his arms the child had finished his snack and had begun to doze, head lolling against his
caretaker's chest with heavy lidded eyes. You felt your heart warm at the sight of them both,
relaxing as if you had just come home from a very long journey.

"As in...pretty." He supplied at last, and you had to strain your ears to hear the small, quiet
confession whispered against the twilight shadows of the courtyard.

You felt yourself breathe in sharply, entirely unprepared for the remark. Your eyes went wide,
heartbeat stammering in your chest as his voice resonated in your thoughts. Lips parting in a
silent realization, you looked at the hunter in front of you lit in a gentle halo by the courtyard
lamp. The soft yellow glow reflected on his armor, glinting off the black of his visor as it
stared back at you unflinching.



Distantly, you wished you could stay in this moment forever. You wanted to stay suspended
in the moment between his confession and when he would dance away again, forbidding
himself from staying too close. If only you could live like this forever, you thought, hanging
in this moment where the cool evening breeze tickled your warm cheeks and the shower of
petals fell between the two of you. Maybe then you could take a step closer, try to see the
eyes beneath Din's helmet as they gazed back into you.

Yet at the same time you could feel an inevitable recognition wash over your thoughts,
warming you from tip to toes. That small part of you, the one that whispered his name to
yourself in a secret confession against the dark of night now embraced you gently. All the
while Din stood before you, cape swaying gently in the breeze even as he remained still like a
silent protector.

Oh. You realized softly, and the thought shone down on you like sunlit clouds parting after a
serene rainstorm. That's what it is.

-ARC THREE: CORUSCANT, COMING IN APRIL-



Chapter 19: Part Nineteen: The Message
Chapter Summary

It was the same. Just as you had been afraid to admit your own emotions hidden within
your heart, Din couldn’t bear to admit the truth to himself either. You gazed up at him as
if looking into a mirror, silently seeing yourself but imagining him.

The thought that you had tried to ignore just as Din had ignored you now shone through
with true colors. Like light through a prism, your feelings now revealed themselves in
dazzling vibrancy. You had tried to deny it, couldn’t bear to give that emotion a name.
The reason you had been so upset, had let your doubts fester and hurt you so deeply now
became clear.

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

Time passes slowly in space, you learned.

The Razorcrest is different when it isn’t parked on a planet. It’s louder, the engines a constant
thrum against the walls and under your feet. Yet it is still in the way that only space can be,
devoid of sound, light. There’s no noise outside the hull, and in some ways the void swallows
some of the sound inside the ship as well. The air is motionless around you at all times,
holding its breath in an ever unknown anticipation. Like a crystal-clear pool, every motion or
noise that you made ripples against your senses.

Din had parked the ship in orbit above a recluse moon in an otherwise gas-giant filled
system. The location was out of the way, and the presence of the gaseous planets confused
sensor and tracking arrays, which kept you three safe from any pursuers, be them Imperial
hunters or Guild members. It meant that even though you were hiding, you three could
breathe a little easier knowing just how hard your enemies would have to work to find you.

It had been at least a week since your departure from Rishi, if you were tracking your hours
correctly. Your heart still swelled with the memory of the village, complete with their rescued
children, waving goodbye to you, Din, and the child as you lifted up into the atmosphere. The
ever-pink horizon on the tropical planet had slowly faded into a hazy atmosphere that gave
way to the black void of space. The glittering lights of hyperspace soon followed, your eyes
reflecting the dazzling blue light from your seat in the cockpit.

Yet without the presence of the blazing Rishi sun and soft purple twilights, you had quickly
found your schedule muddled. With no way to tell time other than the malfunctioning
chrono-keeper in the cockpit, it was difficult to discern a proper schedule of sleeping, eating,
and spending you time fixing the interior of the Razorcrest. Time was an abstract in space,



one you couldn’t truly be bothered to grapple with. You had sorted out a small schedule,
making sure to prepare food for yourself and the child at regular intervals, and to get sleep
when you felt the urge. Other than that, however, time was what you made of it whilst the
ship floated in the stillness of space.

Much like the moon you had stationed yourselves above, you and Din maintained an
unbalanced gravitational pull with each other.

Something had...shifted between you both after your departure from Rishi. Whereas you had
grown increasingly comfortable with the Mandalorian, often inviting him to talk or join you
with the child, Din had grown increasingly distant. He would refuse your invitations, choose
to spend much of his time by himself, and had once again built an invisible wall between you
two. The change both surprised and disappointed you, as you thought you had finally earned
an easy companionship with the hunter.

It wasn't as if he didn't trust you. If anything, Din's approval of your repairs tinkering with his
beloved gunship indicated you had earned his confidence in you. Yet since the moment inside
the hold of the Razorcrest, that moment where you two had spoken in low voices and had
tended to each other’s wounds, Din had tried to put as much space in between you two as
possible. His former habits of joining you as you and the child ate, offering small bits of
conversation and being present in your company, had tapered off into nothingness. Now he
spent his time holed up in the cockpit, coming out only when you asked for his advice with
repairs or for some form of sustenance.

It baffled you, this change. More than that, it brought forth an uncertain anxiety in your chest
you couldn't quite place. The possibility that you had somehow offended him, had done
something to lose the odd friendship you two had built plagued you. The idea that Din was
purposefully avoiding you ate away quietly inside you, even as you tried to reassure yourself
that he was simply on guard, making sure the ship hadn’t been detected. Yet as the days
turned into a full week without a full conversation with the Mandalorian, your fears
multiplied every time you lay to sleep and woke to find things unchanged.

You had tried to approach him about it, tried to ask what you had done or attempt to
understand the sudden shift in his behavior. Yet every time you posed the question Din
retreated further into himself, finding an excuse to escape your vicinity in the tiny spacecraft.
Before you could pressure him, before you could try to pin him down, he would vanish and
lock himself in the cockpit.

In all aspects this was probably for the best, to maintain an exclusively professional
relationship as you tried to earn your keep and Din kept you three safe from the Guild and the
Imperial Remnants. Yet every time Din drew away from you as if under enemy fire, the stiff
nods and tight, modulated voice he gave you made your stomach sink farther and farther into
a pit of uneasiness.

The few moments he did allow you, when he would thank you gently for bringing him food
or reminding him to rest let that ache slowly dissipate. Like a gentle rain washing everything
clean, that tone he used only for you made you sigh in relief.



Your own reaction to such instances puzzled you in some ways. You didn't know when you
had started desiring this attention, this soft validation in the form of thanks or approval with
your work. Every time Din did let his gaze settle on you, let his shoulders relax for all of a
moment you felt yourself relax in turn, like binary stars settling into a cosmic dance of
balance.

You had felt the same way on Rishi, in that moment where you two had stood in the flowered
alcove with the lanterns casting a warm yellow light upon your forms. You could still smell
the sweet floral essence of the air, feel the breeze tickle your skin as you gazed at the Mando
in front of you holding the sleeping child in his arms.

You still hadn't fully understood his words from then: pretty, he had called you. More than
once the sound of his voice, the way he had said the words appeared in your thoughts
unbeckoned. It made a warmth rise to your face and sent a small shiver along your spine.

Something in you had changed too, since then. You couldn't exactly place it, but you felt it
nonetheless. It was in the way your eyes lingered on Mando's broad back while he was
turned, the way you imagined what color his eyes were under the helmet. When you slept the
name he had confessed to you, Din, tempted your thoughts with its simple and yet somehow
intimate sound. When he was close to you in the hold you could feel yourself tense, feel
yourself suck in air whilst wondering what his shoulders and arms were like without the
armor. More than once you wished you could reach out and touch him.

There were moments when you came closer to understanding. When you bent to inspect a
panel and found Din following your gaze, so close you swore you could hear his heartbeat
under his chest plate. In the moments when you two orbited ever closer, coming within a
breath of each other without realizing, then looking up to discover the other had closed the
distance, you could feel your air stutter in your chest.

You didn't want to admit the name of that odd sensation you got when he was close by, the
way your heartbeat thrummed louder in your ears and you automatically felt your muscles
loosen in relief. It was there, ever present just as the idling hum of the Razorcrest's engines.
Yet to name it meant you would be forced to reconcile your own feelings against Din's refusal
to interact with you, drawing ever in on himself and further away from that warmth in your
heart.

So instead, you threw yourself into the arduous task of correcting minor repairs here and
there aboard the ship. Your task was aided by the purchase of proper repair tools, ones gifted
to you upon your departure from Rishi. Slowly, over the course of many hours, you had
managed to make progress. The panel that didn't close right here was now secured, the loose
wire in the floor was now reconnected, and the control panel frame now longer wobbled
under your touch.

Most important, however, was the repair of the 'fresher on board.

It had taken some time to pin down the issue, which in the end turned out to be a mutual
malfunction in the filtering system as well as the pressure valve. With Din's help you had
managed to drain the tank and reset the system. Within a few days the tank had filtered and
refreshed itself, and you were able to enjoy your first ever shower aboard the Razorcrest.



Even though the water was recycled (and treated), even though the showers were short and
not particularly warm, to enjoy one brought you a sense of pride at being able to fix one of
the worst issues aboard the ship. It was also much more efficient than trying to bathe in the
Rishii lagoons and having to worry about wildlife and all sorts of unpleasant plant matter at
the bottom of the pool.

Not to mention that the lock on the inside of the door meant no possibility of accidental
onlookers.

You buried your face in your hands at the memory, the water cupped within them splashing
onto your skin. The shower head beeped above you, warning you of the time limit on its
supply. Rivulets of water raced down your back as you tried to swallow down the flustered
warmth on your face.

You had almost forgotten the memory of Din's choked voice speaking to you from the
underbrush, of trying to cover as much of you as possible while he insisted he had looked
away. You wanted to groan in embarrassment despite the fact that it had happened weeks ago.
Neither of you had discussed it any further once Din had returned to the village that same
afternoon. Yet even now you could feel goosebumps race along your skin with the knowledge
that he had seen you. More than that, you struggled with the idea that in some ways, you had
liked it.

The shower above you beeped once more, and after a moment the water tapered off with a
low hiss. You were left dripping in the standing room only shower, hands still cupping your
face as the sound of running water faded and you could once again hear the low thrum of the
engines. You dragged your palms down your face, skin slick against your touch. Again, the
memory of your exposed form perched on the edge of the lagoon, of the strain in Din's voice
filtered through your thoughts, followed by the soft intonation of his voice in Raider's Cove.

"As in...pretty."

With a quick shake of your head, you reached for your towel and change of clothes. You
couldn't think about this. It was too much and brought forth an ache in your heart you didn't
know existed until now.

Wisps of warm steam poured from the shower once you opened it, dressed and dried off. You
glanced at your bunk right across from the fresher, took stock of the extra folded blanket that
hadn't been left by you.

Voices filtered beyond the door, and you followed them to the cockpit where Din and the
child were seated looking at the holonet. Din was paying attention more so than the toddler
next to him, who was currently occupied with the small metal orb in his hand. Your entry
made both of them look up in unison, and you tried to ignore the way Din's shoulders
suddenly stiffened, the way he quickly averted his gaze from you.

"Star charts again?" You asked casually, hands still reaching up to dry off your hair with the
towel. You tried to hide the disappointment in your voice at him again trying not to meet your
eyes, fiddling with the same panel you had seen him occupied with every time you entered
into his hideaway.



"Yes." He replied simply, voice even and without emotion. You bit back a frown, muscles
tensing restlessly. It stung, this rejection. After everything you two had gone through together
this sudden turnabout in Din's behavior made you feel like strangers all over again. That
familiar dark creeping shadow in your chest rose into your shoulders, hackles rising at your
companion's refusal to even bother facing you.

"Is the kid bothering you?" You tried instead. "I can take him if he's distracting."

"No, he's fine."

You paused, then replied hesitantly: "Okay, well the fresher is free now if you want it."

"I'm okay for now.”

"…I'll be making some food soon, would you like me to bring you some?"

"No thanks."

"Well, I fixed a vent with some carbon scoring on it, would you want to have a look?"

"I'm sure it's fine." And this time his tone was curt, annoyed at your persistence.

You blinked at his turned form, lips parting in surprise at his abrupt shortness with you.
Mando hardly ever snapped at you, and when he did it was always related to trying to keep
you three safe and out of danger. To hear him become terse with your attempts at
conversation struck you in a way you hadn’t expected.

Something snapped in you then, like a chord drawn much too tight and fraying in the middle.
Yet the emotion that came out of you wasn't annoyance, nor was it anger.

Instead, you asked very quietly: "What did I do, Din?"

You were surprised at how much the hurt in your voice bled through, like bile rising in your
throat at this sick uncertainty that had been plaguing you for days now. Your stomach
clenched at just how pathetic you sounded, but you couldn't hold back any longer. Din's
constant avoidance and cold shouldering had cut you in ways you didn't want to admit, and
you had let it fester like a raw wound. Now the change in Din’s voice had exposed it like a
raw nerve, shooting a sharp ache through you at just how much you couldn’t stand his
attitude.

Din paused at your words, his hand hovering above a button on the console before he turned
sharply to look at you. The motion made you flinch, afraid that his previous annoyance
would now rise to frustration at your constant pestering. Yet his entire body went taut, hands
reaching for you before he suddenly stopped himself. He froze, holding himself stiffly even
as he had halfway reached out to touch you. Again, it looked like he was at war with
something inside him you couldn't see, something he wouldn't let you look at even if you
pried.

The silence that followed made your shoulders tremble, and inwardly you cursed at yourself
for appearing so weak. He was only ignoring you, you tried to tell yourself. You had lived



through much worse. Yet the fact that it was him made you wrap your arms around yourself,
as if the air surrounding you had gotten a touch too cold.

"I'm sorry if I've been annoying." You started, and your voice cracked with how tightly you
had wound yourself. "I don't mean to be. I just...don't understand why you suddenly won't
talk to me. I don't know what I did, if I offended you or somehow made you angry- if you
could just tell me, then maybe- maybe I could try to fix it. I-"

"Cuyan, no-" And when he called you that, by that name he had given you, survivor, you felt
even worse. You had earned that title for being strong, for fighting and clawing your way out
of horrific situations in a desperate attempt to survive. Yet here you were, eyes growing hot
with tears at just how deeply you were wounded by a little bit of shirking from someone you
had considered a friend.

"Then what?" You asked sharply, and your voice rose enough to make the child in the seat
beside you look up in concern with large brown eyes. "What did I do to make you want to
avoid me so much? I didn't mean to-"

Without warning, Din stood. You took a step back out of an instinct of self-preservation,
suddenly afraid of your protector. His figure towering over you reminded you once more of
the fact that he was a highly lethal, fully capable hunter. His larger frame daunted you as it
had all that time ago when he had discovered you aboard his ship.

You ducked your head, avoiding the gaze of his black visor. Din paused once more, realizing
he had startled you. After a moment he pressed forward once more. Yet he moved slowly,
gently, giving you space to back up and walk away if you needed it. When he reached out,
when his gloved hands landed on your upper arms, you felt your entire body go loose with
his touch.

"I'm sorry." He said at last, voice lowering so only you could hear. "I didn't mean to be unfair
to you."

You could feel your arms shiver a little under his gloves, and you weren’t sure if it was from
the stress or the fact that the ship suddenly felt so cold. You wanted to run, to put as much
distance between yourself and him, yet you wanted him to be impossibly closer, for those
hands to hold you to his broad chest where you could let your sigh rattle against his armor.

“You’ve done nothing wrong.” He spoke, and his voice was softer now, and indication of
previous annoyance long since fled. “It isn’t anything you’ve done. You…you’re so good to
me, to the both of us-“ and he tilted his head gently down at the basinet where the child
watched both of you with a worried gurgle. “I…I don’t think I’ve told you that enough.”

You kept your eyes down even as his thumb grazed across your bicep. Refusing to meet his
gaze, you felt a bitter expression pass across your face at his words. When you remained
silent, Din continued.

“You don’t have to work so hard. I see you repairing the ship, fixing the ‘fresher, making sure
the child is fed and cared for- it’s like you’re trying to prove yourself.” He paused, and you



could feel the hands on your arms stiffened their touch. “You…don’t need to prove your
place here.”

“Then what is it?” You shot back, but your voice lacked the sharpness you wished you
wielded. “Don’t pretend like you haven’t been avoiding me. I know there’s something I’ve
done, you wouldn’t be so upset otherwise-“

“I’m not upset at you.”

You blinked, and the words that you had formed died against your lips. The air in your chest
seemed to freeze as you sucked in a breath, letting Din’s voice in that gentle tone rest softly
in your thoughts. Slowly, feeling your heart flutter against your ribcage like the delicate
wingbeats of a butterfly, you lifted your head to gaze up at him shyly through your lashes.

“You’re not?” You asked mildly, almost bashfully at Din’s confession.

You heard the quick intake of air underneath Din’s helmet, felt him force himself to loosen
his suddenly tight hold on your arms.

“No, Cuyan.” He murmured, and his voice came out as a warm sigh. “Not at you. Never at
you.”

Your teeth sucked in your lip worriedly, and it took your full composure not to avert your
eyes from his all-too direct stare at you.

“Then…why?” You asked, voice small and uncertain.

Din was silent for a long moment. For a split-second you panicked, afraid he was only going
to retreat once more, shoo you out of the cockpit and leave you beyond the threshold shaking
with the dark sinking feeling that had chewed you from the inside out.

“I…” He started, then paused. You could feel that war within him, could sense the way he
struggled to overcome the doubts within himself to tell you the truth that laid therein. You
didn’t know the source of this turmoil, didn’t know what had forced him into the shadows
away from you. And in some ways you were almost too nervous to ask.

Finally, Din sighed. The sound rattled in his voice modulator. Then, quietly, low enough that
you had to strain to hear him he spoke.

“I was afraid.”

You looked up at him directly now, and your eyes widened at the sudden yet familiar feeling
in your chest at his words. It was like Rishi all over again, with his soft confessions and
posture so relaxed and open. Yet this time he was closer, so close and yet not nearly close
enough. The hands that rested against your upper arms felt warm against your skin, cheeks
hot despite the cool air. That urge to touch him, to open him to yourself rose in your chest and
you couldn’t bear to push it down. You could see your eyes reflected in his visor, bent so he
could meet your gaze open with the emotions you held so tightly to your heart.



Afraid, he had said. Afraid of what? Of you? Of being near you? Talking to you? Hearing
your voice? Afraid of saying something and ruining things? Of seeing you so close and yet so
far-

Oh.

It was the same. Just as you had been afraid to admit your own emotions hidden within your
heart, Din couldn’t bear to admit the truth to himself either. You gazed up at him as if looking
into a mirror, silently seeing yourself but imagining him.

The thought that you had tried to ignore just as Din had ignored you now shone through with
true colors. Like light through a prism, your feelings now revealed themselves in dazzling
vibrancy. You had tried to deny it, couldn’t bear to give that emotion a name. The reason you
had been so upset, had let your doubts fester and hurt you so deeply now became clear.

It was because it was him. It had always been him.

You felt your lips part, the realization echoing past them with a silent stuttering exhale.

Above you, Din watched your expression change, as he could see the epiphany in your gaze.
He stiffened almost imperceptibly, and you wouldn’t have noticed unless you were only a
breath away from each other. The hands that cradled your arms slackened but did not release
you. Instead, they drew you just a little closer, grazed a little higher up to your shoulders-

The sudden, jarring echo from the console startled you both, making the two of you nearly
levitate in surprise. For a brief moment you gazed up into Din’s visor, gasping in a
combination of shock and being overwhelmed at how he had gotten close without even
moving-

You could see Din shake his head once, sighing loudly before releasing you. The sudden rush
of frigid air in the absence of his touch made you shiver. He turned from you to the console,
bending over the array of buttons and panels to find the source of the alarm. You tried to
catch your breath with his back turned, suddenly dizzy at the silent revelation that had
occurred between you two. When you saw Din’s shoulders tighten, saw the way he froze as
he examined the communications panel, however, you felt the last of your air leave your
lungs.

“What is it?” You asked, wincing at the sudden hoarseness in your voice. “What’s wrong?”

It took a moment for Din to reply, and he cast a glance over his shoulder at you before hitting
a button to silence the alarm.

“It’s an incoming message.” He offered at last. “It’s on an encrypted frequency.”

You felt your eyebrows raise towards your hairline at the information. Blinking, you tried to
remember if you had given the Razorcrest’s comm frequency to Arvod or any of the Rishi
villagers. Before you could recall, Din continued.



“I know this frequency.” He spoke, and you could sense his dawning realization through his
words. “It’s a hidden channel used only for Mandalorians.”

That piqued your interest, and soon the thought of Din’s soft touch gliding to your shoulders
was a distant memory. Instead, you sat down in the passenger seat opposite of the child,
leaning over to scoop him up when he beckoned with tiny green hands.

“Mandalorian?” You echoed, and when the child babbled for attention you kept your eyes on
Din. “But I thought-“

“There’s a few of us.” Din provided, interrupting you. “A network of coverts hidden out of
sight, surviving after the Empire ravaged Mandalore. This frequency is only used to signal
other coverts in case they are compromised or under attack.”

You could see Din’s hand hover above the panel, and when you looked closely you could see
the slight tremble in his reach. Yet it was gone in an instant, and for a moment you wondered
if you had even seen it at all.

With a single button press, the comm channel opened and a flickering blue holo-figure
appeared on the console.

It took a moment for the image to stabilize, the voice choppy and robotic for a few more
moments before the signal came through clearly. When it did, you could make out the image
of a broad Mandalorian, larger than Din with heavy armor on all sides. A small repeating
blaster hung from his right shoulder, the ammo coil snaking around to his left elbow and
further to his back. His arms were crossed, helmeted head tucked slightly towards the
communicator.

“This is Paz Vizsla, of House Vizsla, contacting all known covert frequencies.”

“Vizsla?” Din murmured beside you, and despite the low volume of his voice you could hear
the shock than ran through him.

“If this message has managed to reach you, then the Mandalorian covert on Coruscant has
come under attack and is in need of reinforcements. We require immediate assistance from
any members of House Vizsla receiving this message.”

“Coruscant?” You echoed, peering over Din’s chair down at the message. “There’s a
Mandalorian covert on Coruscant?”

Din did a half-shake of his head. “I wasn’t aware of any coverts within the deep core.” He
replied uneasily. “But I do know this Mandalorian. My caretaker was a member of House
Vizsla before he passed away.”

You glanced from the communication to the Mandalorian in the chair in front of you, and a
part of you wanted to ask more about his covert, about his ‘caretaker.’ Now was not the time,
you decided.



“I repeat, I call upon the aid of any members of House Vizsla receiving this message. If you
can hear this please proceed to Coruscant at these coordinates. We are in need of-“ You
watched as the message began to fizzle, the image of the broad Mandalorian fraying at the
edges and the sound becoming less distinct. Even when Din bent to try and refine the signal,
the message was garbled, unclear. Eventually he closed the frequency, leaving the two of you
in the silence that was left by the absence of the Mandalorian’s voice.

You looked at Din, meeting his gaze as he too glanced at you. Neither of you spoke, both
trying to process what you had just heard.

An uneasy weight settled in your stomach, different than the anxiety that had drawn darkly
against your thoughts for the past week. You couldn’t place it entirely on the message you
had just witnessed, the feeling bleeding out from around you into the void of space itself.

“I have a bad feeling about this.” You confessed, and Din nodded slowly in agreement.

“Something isn’t right.” He agreed. “Last time I checked Paz Vizsla was in the outer Rim on
Nevarro. I have no idea how he got so far into the core.”

He paused, and you watched him weigh the message’s contents in his mind. You’d be lying if
you said you weren’t curious as to its origins. Din was the only Mando you had ever met, and
the knowledge that there was an entire secret society of them fascinated you. Yet the fact that
an entire covert of highly trained warriors was calling for aid meant that the threat they were
facing would be extremely dangerous not only to you, but to even Din himself.

In your arms the child cooed, reaching up to pat your face as if sensing your unease and
trying to reassure you. You held his tiny grasp against your cheek, eyes not leaving Din’s
form in the seat beside you.

“What are you going to do?” You asked at last, and Din turned his gaze halfway to you.

After a few moments he replied, and his voice was hesitant, unsure. “I don’t want to do
anything that would put you or the kid in danger.” He confessed, and you felt that little flutter
of warmth in your chest once more.

You frowned in concern, brow furrowing with your gaze. “But those are your people.” You
intoned softly, bouncing the child in your arms as he made a small plaintive sound of distress.
“You can’t just leave them.”

Din regarded you, leaning back in his chair to gaze up at you directly. You offered him a
small, consolatory smile.

“Besides.” You went on, summoning a bit of courage. “I’ve always wanted to see Coruscant.”

Din stared at you for a moment longer, almost as in disbelief. The he huffed once, something
akin to a half-chuckle. Resting his gaze on the communications console once more, he
remained silent for a few moments longer before replying.



“Might as well put some caf on.” He remarked exasperatedly, but his voice had softened with
a touch of affection. “It’s going to be a long ride.”
