Din had left the ramp closed, but even so with frigid fingers you managed to punch in the
code he had taught you, the star date he had found Grogu. The ramp creaked open, groaning
in the cold, and the sound alone had you looking back down the path to see if a familiar
beskar-clad figure stood in the snow. Yet you were alone, not even one of the villagers
standing to observe you as you hurried aboard and began to quickly gather anything of yours
that might prove useful. Your tool pack, your toiletries, a change or two of clothes, various
projects you had been toying with that might be worth enough credits to buy a ticket on a star
liner, and...



 

Your blaster.

 

You felt your face fall at the sight of the familiar model planted on Din's cot, as if hastily
placed there and promptly forgotten whilst he dealt with your unconscious form. You had
noticed its absence from your holster earlier, and now you cradled it in your hands, thumb
stroking softly over the chamber as an errant pang of regret stabbed through your chest.

 

Din had given you this. It was the first thing he had ever provided you with, on that nameless
moon where you had once told him your name at the start of your travels with him. It felt like
a lifetime ago now, the days and months within his presence blurring just like the light of
hyperspace. Just how long ago was it that he gave this to you? Just how long ago had you
accepted it with an oath to protect his charge, to keep Grogu safe? Just how long had it been
since Din's hands had settled on yours, firmly directed your aim as his voice murmured in
what had then been such a near proximity that it left you nearly dizzy with the after-effects?

 

You closed your eyes, forcing yourself to breathe through the sob that threatened to bubble up
your throat. Exhaling shakily, you holstered the blaster again into its place at your side,
whispering a silent apology that you would only take this one thing from him. Everything
else you would leave behind, would abandon just as you would him, here on this icy world
that had managed to freeze the recesses of your heart into something untouchable.

 

You weren’t sure which was worse: the thought of being killed for what you were, or the
thought that it could be him. Worse yet was the idea that Din might simply leave you here,
abandoned on this desolate frozen land on your own, never to see him or Grogu again for all
your years.

 

You had been alone before. You knew what that was. It was reaching out in the darkness and
imagining a form there sleeping beside you, looking up from your meal and daydreaming of a
simple conversation with someone nearby. It meant sitting in the evening air as the sounds of
the city droned on around you and wishing that someone, anyone, might bump their knees
against yours, whisper your name just once.

 

It meant not having this emptiness inside of you that seemed to expand with every passing
year, every month, every day until you hoped someday someone might come fill it.

 



You had found it, the source to filling that silent longing inside you. It had been unexpected
but not unwelcome, a chance coincidence that had spiraled into something greater than
yourself, than him, than you both. This feeling between the two of you was too great to
describe, painting the world in colors you had never dreamed to imagine and bolstering you
in ways you had yet to discover.

 

With Din you had become so much more confident, so much more certain of yourself. You
had turned from a fugitive to a force to be reckoned with, and then to something that passed
as a vessel for the Force itself. You were sure if you gazed back at the person you had been
when you left Kaddak you wouldn’t even recognize your own terrified figure running,
bolting towards the barest glimpse of survival, of freedom.

 

No, you didn’t even recognize the person that came before that- the small, scared form of a
child standing amidst death and devastation, of fire and fury of an Empire that sought to
destroy all that you were. Yet that same fear still dwelled within you- the fear of death, of the
darkness that came after, of not living to a moment where you could experience unrelenting
happiness just once more.

 

Yet greater than that was the fear that the person who had given you hope again would be the
one to issue the killing blow- lest he leave you broken without him for the remainder of your
life.

 

So, to spare yourself the consequences of his own decision, you took it upon yourself to make
it for him. If it meant surviving to a day that maybe, one day, you would forget about him,
about ever meeting him, then maybe you could live without the pain of leaving him, of hating
yourself for all that you were to him.

 

Turning, you reached for your pack, but paused when something glinted in the soft overhead
light of the cargo hold. Blinking, your gaze sought out the object, brow furrowed until at last
you found it- a small, shiny thing tucked under a blanket to the back of Din's cot. Curious,
you reached for it despite yourself, fingers gently wrapping around an object smaller than
your palm.

 

You didn't realize what it was for a moment, surprised by the reflective, almost iridescent
shine of the carving, almost like beskar. After a moment, your memories supplied the feeling
of something still wet from the ocean, pressed into Din's open palm as he turned it in the
sunlight.



 

The shell.

 

You felt your lips part, surprised that he had even remember such a small trinket from your
brief time on that waterside planet. Yet more surprising was the way it had been molded,
soldered at the edges and whittled down precisely into a symbol more familiar, more sacred.

 

A mythosaur skull.

 

Again, your mind flashed back, raking over time and distance back to the same symbol you
had seen on Coruscant, graffitied on a wall, engraved on a pauldron, hoisted above a tunnel
with a guard on either side. The symbol of Mandalorian culture, an ancient and sacred
emblem that spoke for generations of warriors.

 

Your heart clenched, and again you replayed those words Din had spoken in the cockpit
above you, voice soft and touch tender.

 

"I...wanted to make you something out of it." He said at last, voice tinted with a small rasp.
"If you'd let me."

 

You blinked, watching him fidget with the shell for a moment before finding your voice:

 

"What will you make?"

 

Din glanced up at you, holding your gaze. You tried to envision his eyes underneath: open,
considering, warm.

 

"I don't know yet." He replied at last. "Something beautiful, hopefully."

 

Something beautiful.



 

It was beautiful, you realized. The trinket caught and reflected the light above almost like
beskar. Yet the colors underneath were iridescent, taking on a variety of purple and blue hues
that somehow reminded you so much of him. You could almost hear him whisper your name
as you turned it over in your palm, his breath tickling the shell of your ear as he searched for
that brightness within you in hopes he would bathe in its radiance.

 

Your heart clenched at the memory, and you tucked the pendant close to your body as if it
could somehow ease the pain. Despite the cold wind whipping at your back, of the threat of
Din awakening and discovering you, intercepting your escape, you couldn’t help but feel
tears brim at the corner of your eyes, caught in that hopeless tide of longing towards him.

 

“Please don’t ever leave me.” He had whispered to you, his voice cracking in his throat
desperately, the tone of which you had never heard in him. Despairing, hopeful, lost, and
helpless all at once he had begged you to stay, pleaded with you to never be away from him
ever again. Yet instead, you had simply imbedded the memory of his voice, of his touch, of
his breath and body into your mind and chosen still to let him go.

 

Beautiful, just like him, you thought silently, heart cracking at the seams.

 

Beautiful just like his voice and protective embrace, seeking to shield you from all that
sought to hurt you. Beautiful, like his unwavering presence at your side, at the way he echoed
his name for you, at the sight of his unforgettable silhouette in the moonlight. Beautiful like
the taste of his lips upon yours as you kissed him, let your fingers comb through his hair in
the darkness. Beautiful like the stars that burst between you both as you reached for each
other in the midnight, two wounded hearts desperately seeking each other in a galaxy full of
uncertainties. Beautiful like the way he had whispered a plea to you to stay, to never leave
him ever again.

 

Beautiful like him, beautiful like you, beautiful like the thing that existed between you both.

 

Beautiful like love.

 

…Gods above, what had you done?



 

The tears against your face scorched your skin like the fire from your memories, tracing
rivulets of flame against your cheeks as your voice poured from your throat in a sudden
choked cry, clutching the pendant to your chest like a life raft as you were swept out to sea.

 

You were leaving him.

 

You were abandoning him, abandoning your clan, leaving your home. Instead, you were
again choosing your own survival, trying to eke out a modest existence in this galaxy in a
desperate bid for one more day, one more hour, one more chance for happiness despite this
unrelenting and horrific heartbreak.

 

...All whilst leaving behind the only place where you had ever felt true, unbridled joy.

 

You had run that day too, you realized. Even now you remembered sprinting away from
flames and fire, from darkness and from ruin in hopes that despite that tragedy, maybe one
day you could be happy again. Yet now that you had truly found it, now that you were here,
you were fleeing once more in an innate instinct to protect yourself.

 

How many times would it take? How many times would you have to run from your own life
just to preserve it, to protect yourself? Would you ever be this happy again?

 

Cuyan.

 

Survivor. That name seemed hollow when it had poured from his lips last night, a mockery of
your own decision to leave him, fearing that the truth might bring it all crashing down on
you. You had survived after the night that would have been your execution, but it had been a
hollow existence, a lonely one. Yet then you had found Din, had found your clan, and bit by
bit your miraculous survival became less of a miracle and more of destiny, bringing you to
the place you were always supposed to be, there in his arms.

 

Survivor, Jedi, Stowaway.



 

You.

 

You knew now. Din would never hurt you. Not even over this.

 

You couldn’t leave him. Not now, not ever. Your place was with him, now and forever.

 

You had to go back.

 

A creak sounded behind you, steps coming aboard the Razorcrest gently, almost hesitantly.
You could feel your heart sing out to him, tears in your eyes as you turned with an apology, a
confession ready on your lips about everything. Your memories, your identity, your fears and
nightmares, your desperate, unyielding, mesmerizing love for him that seemed destined by
the stars themselves.

 

 

 

 

 

You barely caught sight of who it was before the sound of a stun fired from a blaster rang out,
electrified your body for a single moment in a blue blaze of light. Muscles abruptly spasming
then failing, you felt yourself cave, heard your body impact the floor of the Razorcrest with a
harsh thud that you barely felt.

 

The pendant tumbled from your grasp as your hand went slack, but the sound of it clattering
to the floor was obscured by the harsh footsteps that echoed across the durasteel floor as your
attacker approached you.

 

Yet the final word on your lips, whispered in a desperate silence as your vision faded into
nothingness was:

 



"Din."

 

 

 

----

 

 

 

"Din."

 

Din's eyes opened slowly, body heavy and mind sluggish as he chased the sound of your
voice through his lingering dreams. He could still feel you, could feel your body pressed
under his, fingers entwined, and legs tangled under the sheets. The scent of you still filled his
nose, buried into the junction of your throat and shoulder as he gasped out your name, and in
return your lips spilled an endless, heavenly chorus of small cries and pleasured whimpers.

 

The guilt, the uncertainty that had plagued him last night seemed dimmed in the gentle
embrace of morning, tucked under the sheets and greeted by the utter silence of the remote
mountain village. It didn't matter now, not after last night when he had taken you in his arms
and broken himself apart to you, catching the shattered pieces of you in turn.

 

When Din's eyes took in the dawning light through the windows he automatically reached for
his face to ensure his helmet was in place long before anyone had the opportunity to see his
face. Yet instead, his hand raked over his bare expression, fingers grazing the unshaved
stubble trimming his jaw. He sighed, both in torpor and disappointment.

 

Too tired to panic just yet, Din fumbled towards the edge of the bed, fingers fortunately
clasping around a familiar beskar dome and dragging it towards him. Had he not been so
exhausted, so sated, perhaps he would have lashed out at himself for being so careless, for
allowing himself to sleep to such an hour where someone else might chance upon his face
without him knowing.

 



Yet at the same time, the thought that it was you...

 

Din sighed again, the sound familiar through the filter of his helmet. It was only once it was
fully situated atop his face that he turned to his other side, reaching out a hand for you. He
expected your form to greet him, buried under blankets and burrowed there after your
combined late hour activities. Already his mind summoned the image of your form, tucked
away from him and hogging the blankets to retain that much more warmth to your bare body.
Lips parted, face slack, hair messy and sprawled across the pillow under your head. Beautiful
and lovely and strangely arcane in the mysteries you kept so stubbornly hidden from him.

 

Yet all that greeted Din was an emptiness where you belonged.

 

"Cuyan?" Din echoed at once, voice creaky with sleep. He looked beyond the bed, ignoring
the stab of fear at the thought you had seen his face without his permission and instead
searching for you. Yet all Din received in turn was silence, your voice and presence entirely
absent from the room of the cold, aging inn.

 

Din sat up now, scanning the room for any trace of you. The doors to the balcony hadn't been
unlocked, and from Din's vantage you were not standing outside and observing the dawn
spread across the mountain tops. Nor were you huddled by the fire that had long since gone
out, trying to poke alive flames there. A glance to the bedside table proved you had taken
your change of clothes, likely into the fresher.

 

Din followed suit, muscles much too lax for his liking, treated to a long rest on the most
comfortable mattress he had felt in months. A roll of his shoulders yielded several pops of his
joints. Yet Din ignored them, sitting up and dragging the scattered remains of his clothes to
him. He didn't put on his full armor just yet despite the chill, and in truth it was partly due to
the hope that perhaps you might rejoin him in bed, sleep for just a few more minutes in his
arms.

 

A knock on the door of the bathroom rang out hollowly, and even when Din echoed your
name he heard no response. He couldn't even hear the sound of the sink or shower running,
couldn't even sense the presence of another person there. Drowsiness abandoned him now,
replaced by a sudden, sharp concern at your absence. To confirm his fears, the fresher was
empty when he opened it, pristine and hardly touched.

 



It was only then that Din noticed your jacket, your bag, your boots were missing. Just like
you.

 

"Cuyan." Din whispered, horror now blooming inside him. Yet it was stifled by the pressure
of denial, refusing to believe for a single moment that you had just left without a word.
Surely you were just downstairs in search of breakfast, or maybe went to go retrieve
something from the Razorcrest.

 

That had to be it. You just went to fetch some shower items maybe, an extra blanket, or
maybe a project to fiddle with. There was no way you had simply walked out, had...

 

Yet something in Din's memories brushed against his thoughts, the words and touch gentle
but voice bittersweet as it lay against his sleeping thoughts.

 

"I will always love you."

 

Why had your words sounded like a goodbye?

 

Din wasted no time in gathering his armor now, movements calculated and practiced. He
tried to ignore the way his hands shook as he tugged on his flight suit, attached his pauldrons,
secured his vambraces. The mere process of donning each layer felt too long, too tedious, and
with every fumbled movement he feared perhaps you had taken that moment to put that much
more distance between you and him, vanishing into the snaking mountain paths beyond the
village.

 

Din's imagination ran wild despite himself, conjuring images of your form obscured by the
snow, never once turning back, never again looking at him with those eyes he had come to
love so dearly.

 

At the same time a smaller hurt, sharper and fiercer, lurked and growled beneath that fear. It
twisted and churned low in his stomach, dark and rotten at the idea you had left without so
much as a goodbye, had simply abandoned him after you had spent the night crying into his
arms, pressed into the mattress under him, legs tangled with his and moaning his name.



 

The child made a whine when Din opened the bassinet, protesting being awoken at such an
early hour. Din cradled him carefully for a moment, watching his eyes blink and adjust to the
growing light of sunrise that filtered in through the frosted windows. Yet like Din he seemed
to note his other caretaker's absence quickly, ears perking and head turning in search of your
missing figure. He looked at Din, words absent but a small, plaintive 'awah?' in query.

 

"I'm sure she's just at the ship." Din told him as he finished gathering his things, a tremor
barely audible in his voice but still present. The words were meant to reassure the child just
as much as they were meant to comfort himself, trying to push down the horrid, nearly
sickening thought of your departure.

 

"C'mon kid." Din nodded, setting the bassinet to follow him out of the room and down the
stairs, past the small lobby and warmly lit kitchen, out into the snow. His steps were quick,
purposeful, eyes instantly scanning for any trace of you. A press at the side of his helmet
yielded his infrared vision, the typical orange footprints of others flickering a cool green
against the icy street. Yet between them lay a brighter path, undistracted and headed directly
towards the edge of town.

 

To the Razorcrest.

 

Din wasted no time, keeping his pace measured so as to not only assuage suspicion of his
strange figure in the village, but to reassure his own hammering heartbeat.

 

You were just picking something up from the hold, he told himself again. You were fetching
perhaps a hairbrush or a warmer outer layer, something Din had forgotten to bring for you the
day before. He would get to the ship and find you rummaging through a bin or perhaps a
panel behind the cockpit, and when he arrived you would give him that smile you always did,
would echo his name in that way he loved so desperately.

 

Yet Din's stomach seemed to only drop further downwards when the Razorcrest came into
view at the edge of the village, its ramp open but no motion apparent from the distance at
which Din stood.

 



Din broke into a sprint now, anxiety overcoming him and veins cold not from the chill, but
from the fear that this nightmare of his had chased him into reality. Face drawn tight under
his helmet, eyes wide, he burst into the cargo hold with your name on his lips, abandoning
the title he had given you in favor of calling out for you in panic.

 

Again, your voice did not return to him, and as Din listened he didn't hear the echo of your
footsteps above in the cockpit, didn't hear another sound of living life besides himself and the
child beside him. Din called again, voice rising in alarm now, attempting to refuse the idea
that you weren't here, that he had no idea where you could possibly be.

 

He scaled the ladder faster than he had in his entire life, the motion taking only a mere breath
before he stood in the empty cockpit, looking through the viewfinder out at the snowy
wasteland. Even there he did not see a single figure in the snow, didn't see another living
being for miles down the icy slopes.

 

Every possible scenario began to play through his thoughts. You were in a different house in
the village, he had missed you somehow as he exited the inn, you had taken a stroll in the
snow to admire the crystalline landscape. Yet each possible theory was negated by the
footprints he had followed here, and by the devastating lack of you.

 

“No.” Din thought silently, desperately, pleading with the stars above that this wasn’t the
devastating scenario he that had haunted him for days now like a dark specter. Yet the truth of
it lay as cold against his bones as the frozen, unyielding landscape beyond the ship, the wind
howling a melancholy lullaby for him and him alone.

 

You had left him.

 

You had left him just like he feared.

 

Din gripped the seat in front of him- your seat. His hands clenched over it, knuckles turning
white under his gloves. He blinked underneath his helmet, expression distraught and
confused and betrayed, vainly trying to reconcile his thoughts with reality. The truth of it all
lay cold against his skin despite the layers, as if the beskar plating engraved a freezing brand
onto his body.

 



You were gone.

 

Just like that, just like he had been so terrified of, there and gone again without so much as a
goodbye. Despite his efforts to comfort you, despite pouring his love out to you through his
touch, despite spending the darkness of midnight with you reaching for him, under him,
despite holding you in his arms and whispering his love to you like an oath. You had
vanished.

 

"I will always love you."

 

Had it been a lie? How else could you do this if those words weren't true? If you had loved
him like you said, for what possible reason could you have left him behind?

 

Yet beyond that was the instantaneous guilt, the bite of shame that snarled inside him like
something with fangs at the reason for your absence.

 

It...it was his fault.

 

The thought alone made Din's knees threaten to wobble. Gingerly, hands shaking, he lowered
himself into the pilot's chair, eyes unseeing and grasp trembling on his lap. In the utter silence
of the Razorcrest he had only his thoughts to fill the void, violent and deafening like the force
of a gale.

 

He had done this. He had asked you to stay, his words so selfish back then on Coruscant.
Despite knowing you wanted a simple life, a quiet existence he had asked you to stay, to stay
with him. You had, and it was only because you did that Din was able to to see the
magnificent, ethereal evolution that was you. You were so different from the stowaway he
had found here on the ship all those moons ago, and yet in some ways just the same. Din
wanted nothing more than to continue to see that journey of yours, wherever it led, to listen
to your voice and feel the warmth of you at his side with every step.

 

Yet he had subjected you to so much, had failed to protect you when you needed him the
most. The number of close calls, of barely dodged blaster bullets, of firefights and explosions
and instances of death you had narrowly escaped felt immeasurable. All of them had been as



you had traveled with him, and for what? All so Din could see your smile one more time,
could hear you whisper his name, could feel your fingers entwine in his. He had tried his best
to protect you, had tried to keep you safe, but the life he led was not an easy one, and he had
begun to see the weight of it bearing down on you despite your affections for him.

 

It had been too much for you, and so you had disappeared into the snow, taking with you the
only time where Din had ever felt wholly, truly at home.

 

"Thank you for loving me." He remembered now, those words you had whispered against his
lips before your touch vanished from him completely, absent now and forever.

 

Din let his head sink into his hands, fingers curling into his helmet as he scrunched his eyes
shut, trying to stifle the growing feeling of utter anguish that rose in his chest as it threatened
to steal the air from his lungs. Yet the gesture did nothing, not as Din's heart clenched
painfully around the phantom wound your departure had inflicted there. He knew nothing
would soothe it, that nothing he ever did again would truly rid him of this pain, of this guilt,
this despair that had opened up like an all-consuming, blackened void inside him.

 

He was such a fool.

 

He should have left you on Coruscant, he should have dropped you off in one of the Core
worlds, he should have never asked you to stay, should never have even let you climb aboard
all that time ago. Perhaps, if he had never loved you at all, then this pain, this agony wouldn't
feel as if it was splitting him in two, wouldn't stay with him for all his years to come.

 

"Cuyan." Din whispered, but the name was choked, throat too tight to speak.

 

He had loved you despite himself. He had loved everything about you- the way your brow
scrunched in sleep, the way you fidgeted when toying with one of your projects, the way you
always reached for him so gently, with such tender care and concern. He had loved your
kindness in a world that was rarely kind, had loved the light in your eyes that seemed to
glimmer like the stars themselves. He had loved you, always you, nothing but you, a stray
shooting star that he had caught with open hands, bright and dazzling and his, just as much as
he was yours.

 



Perhaps it wasn't too later- he could find you, but even if he did what would it amount to?
Would you really stay? If you had managed to leave after last night, after his plea panted in
your ears, words desperate, then surely you would leave again. You were determined. Din
might have been able to convince you son some things, but for this? Something that was his
fault and his alone?

 

No. You were gone. He had his chance and he had failed, and now all he had to show for it
were the lonely tracks leading into the snow.

 

If Din could just hold you in his arms one more time, then maybe this pain wouldn't threaten
to devour him alive. If just once more you echoed his name to him with that voice of yours
then maybe...

 

A sound came from below, a small thump and a clatter. Din hardly noticed it at first, head
cradled in his hands and shoulders hunched as he wallowed in his own misery. Flashes of
you, of your smile, your voice, your touch cycled endlessly through his thoughts, and because
of that Din nearly missed the small series of gurgles and whines that echoed from just below
the hatch.

 

"Kid?" Din asked, thoughts jolting and voice cracking as he turned towards the ladder.

 

As if to answer, the child let out an insistent whine, his voice carrying up into the cockpit.

 

Din managed to gather himself, standing despite the sudden fatigue in his bones, the weight
in his chest. He shuffled over to the top of the ladder, peering down as the child seemingly
pointed at something beyond Din's sights, babbling urgently. Reluctantly, Din descended the
latter, carefully not to step on the toddler as he set down.

 

"Now's...not a good time, pal." He offered at last, lifting up the infant and turning towards the
floating bassinet to deposit him there once more. "Just...give me a minute, okay?"

 

Din turned, thoughts still preoccupied as he set himself on his cot. Yet by the time he had
done so the child had once again wrestled his way out of his carrier, dropping to the floor and
urgently skittering off between two small chests to the side of the hold.



 

Din sighed, letting the youngster go, too tired to try and collect him.

 

He was exhausted.

 

Perhaps not in body, considering the rest he had the night before. Din swore he couldn't
remember the last time he had slept so well, drifting so deeply that he didn't even dream. No,
Din's exhaustion came from his spirit, from the reality of loss, of losing one more person he
had cherished, from losing the most important of them all.

 

His parents. His people. The Covert. The Armorer.

 

You.

 

Again, that darkness welled inside him, snaked along his legs and arms with inky tendrils,
threatening to drag him downwards into the abyss. Yet before he could the child again let out
a sound, this time sounding triumphant, before wobbling back into view.

 

He held something up to his mouth, and if Din hadn't been so drained he would have shot to
his feet to make sure the child wasn't chewing on something he wasn't supposed to, that he
wasn't about to choke. To his surprise, however, the child came toddling towards him,
balancing on tiny legs and drawing close until he at last offered to object to his caretaker with
a small 'uwah?'

 

Din blinked, staring down at the small thing clasped in the child's three clawed grip. It took
him a moment before he was able to recognize the object for what it was.

 

The mythosaur pendant. The one he had intended to give you but had never gotten the
chance.

 



Absently, his fingers reached for the place he had been hiding it, under a blanket at the back
of his cot. Naturally, it came up empty, so instead Din reached out and took the small carving
from the child below him, turning it over in his hand with bewilderment.

 

How had it gotten all the way over there? He had kept it well concealed, managed to make
sure it wouldn't accidentally be revealed until the perfect moment. If you had found it, surely
you would have kept it?

 

Something in Din shifted, thoughts clearing just enough for him to again look around the
cargo hold with new clarity.

 

Your tool kit lay on a nearby crate, left despite the fact that you carried it with you almost
everywhere. Beside it lay your welding goggles, tossed carelessly aside despite your careful
diligence to your tools. It was odd that you had left them, considering your trade. You had
purchased them with your own money, so why...?

 

Din stood, eyes beginning to take in the messy state of the cargo hold for the first time, the
way things seemed out of place, the strange indication that someone had perhaps been here.

 

Yet it was your pack, hastily packed and tucked haphazardly behind a panel along with your
blaster, as if to conceal them, that spoke all that Din needed to know.

 

Previous thoughts abandoned, Din's instincts roared to life within him, muscles coiling and
heartbeat thrumming loudly in his ears. This felt like no mistake. Careful as you were, you
wouldn't leave behind things that were so important to you if you had well and truly left.
Something wasn't right.

 

Din flickered on his visor, and to his surprise he found not one but two sets of footprints in
the hold. Yet it wasn't that which was telling of the scene that had unfolded, but the cooling
imprint of a body that had collapsed just short of the cot, right under his feet, only to be
dragged into the snow.

 

Eyes wide and heartbeat deafening now, Din raced outside, once again scanning the
surrounding landscape for any sign of life. Yet the villagers merely regarded him with



surprise, not expecting to see a strange Mandalorian frantically spin around in search of any
indication to where you had vanished.

 

No. Din knew now. This was no coincidence. Left though you had, bag packed and ready to
flee, you had been intercepted.

 

You had been taken.

Chapter 48: Part Forty Eight: No Way Out
Chapter Summary

Now Din almost certainly thought you were gone from him, had chosen to leave him
and Grogu behind. If he thought this was your choice, that you had left of your own
accord instead of being captured the moment you reversed your decision, then maybe he
would simply let you go. Perhaps he would let you leave, not knowing that you were
being taken, instead choosing to wallow in his own heartbreak at your betrayal.

The knowledge that came with that forbidden thought crept across you slowly, tangling
you within an inescapable spider's web of dread. If Din didn't know you had been
abducted, if he didn't know you wanted to return to him, then he wouldn't come for you.
No one would.

No one was coming. You were alone.

More than that, this time there was no chance of escape.

Chapter Notes
See the end of the chapter for notes

 

 

 

 

Someone called your name.

 

That sound, the one you were so familiar with, that had been the sound of your own soul
since the first moments of your birth, called out to you through something you couldn't touch.
It wound around you, clinging to the threads of your muscles and imbedding into your spirit,
resonating there as it found the origin of itself. It plucked against the backdrop of your
thoughts, like a clarendon that roused you from the edge of slumber and again into
wakefulness.

 



You could hardly hear it, lost in a mindless haze of confusion as you tried to discern the
world around you. Everything hurt, limbs frozen and stiff from the cold. Heaviness clung to
the sinews of your muscles, a fierce rigidity that you couldn't shake. Your vision swam before
your eyes, only making out strange hazy shapes and colors that made no sense to you. Yet
between all that you could vaguely discern the feeling of movement, of laying on your side
despite the jostle of something under your form.

 

A groan escaped you as your senses came trickling back to you. The bite of the harsh, snowy
wind sliced against your form, seeping past your scant outer layers and down, deep into your
cooling veins. You could smell moisture in the air, the scent of it filling the back of your nose
with the promise of snow. The creaky, intermittent groan of whatever you were laying on
seemed to screech against your ears as it bumped its way down the frostbitten trail you were
on. You tried to crane your head to see, to try and gather any whereabouts of your location,
but found your muscles unresponsive.

 

Blearily, you tried to make sense of it all, of your sudden circumstances, of being moved to
somewhere you couldn't see, of exactly why you couldn't move.

 

Din.

 

Oh Force.

 

At the memory of being ambushed in the Razorcrest, of being stunned and dropped where
you stood before it all went black crashed over you with such sudden devastation you found
yourself gasping for air, trying to writhe where you lay. At once your vision seemed to clear,
and you found yourself looking at a strange collection of furs and crates around you,
scattered across the same hover-cart you had been dumped upon. Some of them covered you,
as if trying to obscure you from anyone who might gaze into the cart and see the crumpled
form of a person there.

 

Your attempted wiggling only managed to summon a dull, insistent pain that throbbed behind
your eyes. Automatically you moaned in pain, tried to reach up and touch your closed eyes,
only to find your limbs too heavy to lift, your hands bound in front of you with bracers.

 

"Awake, are we?" A voice asked, high but even, flat and apathetic.



 

You stilled, suddenly aware of another presence atop the hover cart, echoing just above where
your head lay on the rusted metal of the cart bed. Yet you didn't respond, holding your breath
in hopes maybe you might buy yourself some more time to think, to scheme a way out of
your captive state. The person above you obviously was whoever had taken you from the
Razorcrest, able to sneak up on you with hardly any effort and steal you away without an
inch of resistance on your part. You couldn't see them, but even so you knew that they had to
be dangerous, skilled enough to subdue you without a struggle.

 

"I can see you, you know."

 

That made you try and crane your head upwards towards the voice, only for that sudden,
horrible ache to rise again, like a sarlacc trying to digest the inside of your head. You
whimpered, hating yourself for the small, pathetic sound that escaped your lips.

 

"I thought so."

 

You waited for the ache to subside, trying to remain as still as possible and breathe your way
through the wave of it. Eyes scrunched shut, mind hazy and limbs unresponsive, you tried to
raise your voice to the person speaking to you.

 

"Wha-what d'you do t'me?" You tried, words slurred and chalky on your tongue like charcoal.

 

Your captor paused, and if you had been able to see her you would have seen her shrug.
"Paralyzed you." She replied simply, tone unbothered. The sound of it was slightly toned,
muffled, as if hidden behind some type of helmet. "Heard a rumor from one of my associates
that you might be force sensitive, so I decided to not take chances."

 

" 'M not...fors senstive." You tried to lie, words entirely unconvincing in your drugged state.

 

Your captor, for what she was worth, huffed a laugh, as if amused by your paltry attempts to
dissuade her.



 

"I sincerely doubt that, hun." She replied flatly. Then she fell silent, and for a moment you
thought that was the end of it, that she had decided that was enough. Yet then she sighed as
the cart jolted under you both. "I am surprised you're awake though. That dose should have
kept you under for our entire ride. Maybe you force users are just built different."

 

You scrunched your brow, one of the only movements available to you at her words.

 

"W-where are we going...?" You asked, cursing yourself for your voice sounding so feeble, so
thoroughly incapacitated. Whatever drug she had tagged you with rendered your restraints a
bit redundant, considering it took most of your concentration to simply configure your senses
to gravity, to summon the most basic of words of which to ask her.

 

"You're the bounty, figure it out." The hunter above you responded, her words lilting with
annoyance, as if she were trying to shoo away a pest.

 

You didn't have to. You already knew. There was only one place you could possibly end up at
this point, only one entity in the entire galaxy that had been chasing after you so devotedly, so
ruthlessly.

 

The Empire.

 

You would have shivered if you had control over your body. Instead, you merely felt a wash
of dread fall across your thoughts like the shadow of an eclipse. A different type of cold
seized you now, one that felt your heart still momentarily in your chest and the world around
you sucked into silence. The image of stormtroopers, with their pristine, white reflective
armor, of TIE fighters screaming across the sky and the ever present grip of a galaxy under
siege seemed to dance behind your closed eyes.

 

“Jedi!!” The Imperial office had screamed, and you could still hear her dying words echo
endlessly in the prison of your mind.

 



You had never taken a stand against the Empire during their reign, too afraid and too bent on
your own survival to even dare think about such an effort. Yet it didn't matter, didn't erase the
fact that to them you were an enemy. To them you were a threat, a symbol of the resistance
against their brutality and horrific, suffocating grip on the galaxy. Even if you ran, even if
you kept yourself hidden, your very existence branded you as a target for the rest of your
days.

 

It didn't make sense. The Empire was gone now, fractured into territorial warlords that
roamed the Outer Rim in hiding from the New Republic. Why they were still chasing you,
why they were still bent on finding Jedi at all failed to follow any form of logic whatsoever.
The war was over, they had lost, so why were they still intent on capturing you, on finding
Grogu?

 

Grogu. You eased, face falling at the familiar reminder of the child, of his wide brown gaze
and settled weight in your arms. The pang of hurt that shot through your heart was almost
enough to make you squirm uncomfortably. The thought that the toddler was being hunted for
the same reason you were, for his mere existence, made something fragile within you shudder
and threaten to crack. He didn't deserve this, didn't deserve to be hunted for simply being
alive. You tried to remember his soft coos, his toothy smile and gentle touch on your face. Yet
even when the sound of him echoed your name that hurt only dug deeper into you,
threatening warmth at the corner of your eyes.

 

"Why just me?" You asked aloud, abruptly, voicing your question of why only you had been
taken, considering Grogu had been only a mere walk away from you. The idea that the
toddler might have been captured as well was horrifying, unsettling, and for a moment you
were undeniably grateful that it had been you, only you, and not him.

 

There was silence as your captor considered your question, the cart under you both groaning
as it rattled down the mountainside trail.

 

"Half a bounty is better than no bounty at all." She answered cryptically, voice briefly
muffled by the sound of the cart and the bite of the wind. "Besides, you were alone, an easy
target."

 

That was true, but there was more to the hunter's words than what she spoke. It almost
seemed as if she doubted her own abilities to bring you both in at once. No, it was that in
order to do so she realized she'd have to fight Din, and win. Belatedly, you realized whoever



this hunter was she was likely younger, less experienced than Din, and realized the older
hunter had the advantage of years and experience over her.

 

It didn't matter. You had been taken before and managed to get free, get back to Din as he
ceaselessly chased after you. It wouldn't be long before he caught your trail and caught up to
you both, freed you once more.

 

Except...

 

He...he wouldn't. Not this time, not after you had left him.

 

You closed your eyes against the overwhelming wash of hurt that followed the thought. It
seemed to splice into you, carve into your chest and make a home there, drawing you down,
down into the darkened void of despair.

 

You had left him.

 

You had abandoned him, had kissed him in a silent farewell after spending the night tucked in
his arms, imbedding the sensation of his touch into your very soul. In your own desperation
to survive his potential betrayal you had chosen to leave, to say goodbye to the only part in
your life where you had ever truly been happy, with him. You hadn't stopped to consider the
fact that Din would never hurt you, so blinded were you by your own fear at the revelations
of your identity, your intrinsic instinct to claw your way to freedom, to survival.

 

Too late had you realized that it wasn't enough to live, but to be happy.

 

Now Din almost certainly thought you were gone from him, had chosen to leave him and
Grogu behind. If he thought this was your choice, that you had left of your own accord
instead of being captured the moment you reversed your decision, then maybe he would
simply let you go. Perhaps he would let you leave, not knowing that you were being taken,
instead choosing to wallow in his own heartbreak at your betrayal.

 



The knowledge that came with that forbidden thought crept across you slowly, tangling you
within an inescapable spider's web of dread. If Din didn't know you had been abducted, if he
didn't know you wanted to return to him, then he wouldn't come for you. No one would.

 

No one was coming. You were alone.

 

More than that, this time there was no chance of escape.

 

There was no way out, not with your hands and feet bound, with the blooming ability of the
Force stolen from you in your drugged, paralyzed state. Not with you at the mercy of the
hunter who had taken you. This wasn't like before, when you had fought the Clawdite with
Din racing to your rescue. This wasn't like when you had been taken by the Black Sun and
struggled your way to freedom with Paz at your side. Din wasn't coming this time. No one
was.

 

The inevitability of your fate seemed to stretch before you like a starlit path, all of the
diverging steps fractured and broken as you drew closer to the imminent danger of your own
surrender to your greatest enemy. Even as you tried to search and desperately sought any
other course, the only route open to you was the one you so desperately didn't want to take.

 

To surrender.

 

Everything in your spirit cried out against the thought, the idea being so entirely antithetical
to who you were. You were a survivor, it was in the name Din so tenderly called you as,
entwined within the fabric of your soul. Yet in the face of inevitability, of no escape you felt
that foundation within you fracture, crack at the seams.

 

You were tired.

 

All your life had been spent running, fleeing. You had run from death since the day you could
stand, feeling the fatal bite of darkness threaten to consume you with every step. You had
forced yourself to forget who you were in a desperate bid for freedom, had erased the trauma
of your own miraculous survival at the hands of the Empire in order to pursue it. Even then
you had tried to run from your own identity when you remembered, had denied it in a vain



attempt to shield yourself from the inescapable shadow of death that nipped at your heels
with every heartbeat.

 

You had never tired, never slowed, intent on fleeing for another day, another hour, another
moment of life that you threw yourself at with such desperation it mirrored the energy of a
dying star. In doing so you had forgotten who you were, had refused to remember all the ones
you had lost, and in turn had lost yourself. Now, that same struggle had cost you both Din and
Grogu as well, both of them gone from you forever.

 

There was something in your spirit that was too exhausted to continue now, after realizing all
you had lost. If this is what it was to survive, to live but lose everything you had held dear,
was it truly a life worth living?

 

Perhaps this was your fate, you realized. This realization of yours, perhaps your life was
always leading to this ,to the moment where you inevitably surrendered, gave up on the
chance of being happy ever again. If this was your destiny, to run and flee for so long only to
sprint headfirst into the jaws of death, then maybe it was best to simply let the strings of fate
pull you to their will, dictate your destiny to where it would inevitably conclude.

 

Maybe it was time to give in, once and for all.

 

The feeling of it was a hollow inside you, empty and silent. Numb as you were, you couldn't
feel the warm spill of tears that at last welled in your eyes and traced down your frozen
cheeks.

 

"You ok back there?"

 

You swallowed, wishing you could curl further into yourself and hide your face from the
hunter's gaze. So instead, you closed your eyes, trying to shift and ignoring the immediate cry
of pain from your body as you did.

 

"Why do you care?" You shot back, but your voice was cracked, raw with emotion.

 



"Because I want to get paid." Your captor snarked back. "And I only get paid half if you've
frozen to death."

 

You grimaced, and the tightness of your expression did little to ease the flow of tears down
your cheeks.

 

"Fuck you." You snapped at last, but the insult lacked the force you wanted behind it. If
anything, it only made your abductor snort with laughter.

 

"You're cute, but I'll pass." She scoffed, the sound crackling from under her helmet. "Talk to
me when you're not drugged."

 

You ignored the jibe, lacking the energy or desire to fight with the huntress. Instead, you
reverted to a frosty silence, turning your senses to the world around you. You were angled so
you could partly see the sky, which had turned from the dusky pink and purple hues of dawn
to an overcast, downy gray that spoke of snow. The wind whistled through the peaks that
towered far above the wagon as it trundled down the rugged mountain trail, clunking along as
the rattling of the frostbitten metal filled the silent gap between you both.

 

It was a beautiful planet, you realized. Harsh, cold, but ruggedly beautiful in a way you hadn't
truly come to appreciate. Perhaps if you had stayed with Din you may have gotten a chance
to admire the beauty of it. The idea of tucking into his side and relishing his warmth as you
both watched the stars beyond the mountain range felt heavy inside your chest, an
omnipresent reminder of his absence. You tried to summon the sensation of it, of falling
asleep in his embrace, but the mere thought threatened to drag you further downwards into
the chasm of despair inside you.

 

So caught were you in your thoughts you almost didn't notice when the huntress above you
yawned loudly, shifting as she wrapped herself further into her layers.

 

"Well, this is boring." She intoned dryly.

 

You scoffed, feeling irritation prickle within you at her complete and utter apathy to you,
crying as you were. The frustration of it bubbled up your throat before you could catch it.



"Sorry I can't be more entertaining, I'm a little busy being taken somewhere against my will."
You sneered derisively.

 

Strangely, this prompted a bark of laughter from your captor, the sound sharp as it rattled off
the cliffsides.

 

"I knew you had nehutyc, jetii." She replied, and you mentally berated yourself for playing
into her hands and providing her with the modicum of entertainment she was badgering you
for. Then you blinked, brow furrowing as you recognized the sharp, lilting consonants of her
the word she used.

 

"You know Mando'a?" You asked abruptly, and suddenly you were met with silence as your
captor realized her mistake in letting the word slip. Then she sighed, and you felt the cart
shift with her movement.

 

"You could say that." She answered enigmatically, and if you had the ability you would have
twisted and  narrowed your eyes at her, maybe even caught a glimpse of her face. Instead,
you were forced to stay still, shoulder colliding uncomfortably with the metal center of the
hover-cart. It tilted at a strange angle for a moment, and you contained a yelp before it
corrected itself as it began to descend at a perilous angle. It took you a moment to notice that
you had somehow been anchored to the front of the cart, unable to slip off the back should
you regain control over your limbs. You couldn’t stifle a small expression of admiration over
exactly how thorough the huntress had been before irritation drew darkly across your face
and erased it.

 

"What does it mean?" You asked at last, unable to stand your thoughts filling the frosty
silence between you both.

 

"Hmm?"

 

"Nee...hoo-tish." You tried, tongue warbling over the word.

 

"Nehutyc." The huntress corrected sharply, emphasizing the middle consonant. "It
means...gumption. Guts."



 

You raised an eyebrow despite the fact that the huntress was unable to see it. "How would
you know that about me?"

 

Your captor grumbled, as if scolding herself for being dragged into a conversation with one
of her bounties. "You have to either be brave or stupid to travel with a Mandalorian." She
replied simply, then paused. "Granted, you might actually be stupid with how easy it was to
catch you."

 

" 'm not stupid." You grumbled, irritated, if not a bit chagrined. "-And you're just gloating."

 

"Maybe I am." You could hear the smile sneak into the huntress's voice as she spoke. "Not
every day you catch a jettii."

 

"So, you do know Mando'a."

 

"Tch."

 

Oddly, you smirked to yourself at having managed to annoy your captor. It was a negligible
win at best, but it managed to satisfy you enough to momentarily forget your circumstances.

 

There was silence again for a period, and for a while you thought perhaps your abductor had
given up on the effort of trying to taunt you. Unable to move and having little else to do, you
watched your breath fog into small, billowing clouds before dissipating into the dove gray
sky above.

 

"He teach you?" She suddenly asked, as if she too was unable to bear the silence.

 

You paused for a moment, contemplating.

 



"...Not exactly." You replied honestly, thoughts drawing back to Din’s voice as you
desperately tried to ignore the stab of guilt there. You could hear his voice even now, could
hear him murmur in his language to Grogu, conferring with his brethren in the covert on
Coruscant, responding to Paz’s booming voice with his steady, quiet but commanding tone.

 

For a moment you had to close your eyes, force yourself to breathe against the hurt of it all.

 

"I managed to pick up some here and there, and asked about words he used sometimes." You
offered at last, voice quieter, distracted by memory.

 

The huntress above you huffed. "You two must be close, then." She remarked idly, but you
could hear the slyness barely concealed under her voice. “He your boyfriend or something?”

 

"I-" You tried, feeling a rush of warmth at the reminder of Din and your relationship, briefly
recognizing the memory of you two entwined together last night. "I mean- we...we're- wait."
You frowned indignantly. "W-why does it matter to you?"

 

She snorted this time, your abductor, amused at your embarrassed reply. "It doesn't." She
confessed plainly, but you could hear the undertone of self-satisfied delight there. "Not really,
I'm just curious. Not often you hear about a Mando and a Jedi together."

 

Your face fell, you couldn't help it. The reminder not only of who you were, but that Din
didn't know rang hollow inside you with regret. You never got a chance to tell him, to confess
the reason for your strange turn in behavior, for the nightmares, for the reason you escaped
the outpost, all of it. He didn't know. Now, he'd never get a chance to. Instead he’d be left
with the memory of your final words to him before you vanished like fog into the soft colors
of dawn.

 

“Thank you, for loving me.”

 

Your silence must have been telling, because the energy around you shifted, and at last you
heard the huntress's words pierce your thoughts.

 



"...He doesn't know, does he?" She asked, and her voice was a little solemn now. If you
concentrated on it you could swear you heard something almost skin to regret in her words.

 

"...No." You answered at last, voice hardly a murmur between you. "He doesn't."

 

An odd, subdued quiet fell between the two of you. You didn't expect her to respond. After
all, she was the reason you would never get a chance to tell Din all you had been hiding. You
could sense she knew this, and as a result had no words to offer you despite the small amount
of guilt there.

 

Something cold landed on your cheek, and as you cast your eyes to the sky you watched as
snowflakes began to float gently down from the heavens. They caught against your
eyelashes, and as you blinked they melted into the rivulets where your tears had fallen. You
exhaled, watching your breath fog up and away from you, into the misty mountains, beyond
to where Din remained without you.

 

"Get some rest, survivor." The hunter above you offered, voice subdued. "Best to conserve
your energy while you can."

 

You didn't respond, not to her gentle offer of the way her words felt almost like a confession
of pity towards your fate.

 

The wind whistled sharply against the jagged peaks of your thoughts.

 

---

 

Din looked up to the feather gray sky above him, visored gaze tracing over the silent
descending flakes of snow. Under his helmet he frowned, ignoring the prickle of chill that
managed to permeate through his layers. He let his eyes linger on the clouds above him for a
moment before at last turning his gaze back to the winding mountain path that sloped down
the cliffs ahead of him.

 



It had been hours since he had started tracking you, and despite the time elapsed Din couldn't
stop reprimanding himself for wasting precious minutes before he had given chase. He had to
make sure that the Razorcrest was properly sealed, bribe the local villagers to leave it be in
his absence, and then bribe them more for one of the cart animals to aid him in traversing the
steep, unsteady mountain cliffs. With every minute spent in the village you slipped further
and further from his grasp, like mist through his fingers.

 

It seemed like you had been doing that for a while now.

 

The Orbak under him chuffed impatiently, shifting its weight as Din stared down the trail
before him, jutting downwards into the valley below at a borderline dangerous angle. Din
patted the animal absently, as if trying to reassure his mount as well as his own racing heart.
The uneven, staccato rhythm that had begun after he realized the truth of your abduction had
yet to abate, thrumming unsteadily against his chest plate. His years as a hunter allowed him
to measure himself, keep the panic and anxiety to the periphery of his mind, where it prowled
like haunted shadows.

 

Instead, in its place, Din felt a cold, calculated anger threaten to swallow his senses, lunge
outwards with glowing eyes and sharpened fangs.

 

Whoever had abducted you, whatever their name was, wherever they were, they had made a
fatal mistake in taking you. In taking you from him.

 

Din considered himself a calm man, for the most part. Keeping a level head was a
fundamental requirement of his line of work. Fear, fury, rage were silent killers, fatal
distractions that clouded judgement and awareness. Few things incensed him anymore
beyond the realm of impatience, but this, the fact that this was you-

 

The freezing chill of the mountains was unable to stifle the boil of his blood inside his veins.

 

The idea that you had been stolen from him, that he had been so foolish as to let you simply
vanish from his arms that morning made something itch inside his skin, dark and hungry for
violence. He was furious, furious at himself for letting you go, for not protecting you, for
allowing you to be taken again was almost more than he could bear; and silently, he vowed
that the fool who had dared cross you both would regret the moment they dared lay hands on
you, on his survivor.  



 

A thick layer of clouds to the east hovered at the edge of the valley, like an avalanche of
condensation rolling over the gray and white landscape, threatening to obscure Din's vision of
the trail ahead. A villager had warned him of the deadly ice storms on the planet, gentle at
first until the atmospheric pressure forced ice crystals to harden like frozen daggers that
rained from above. The clouds to the east whispered of such a storm, low and churning like
the grind of the ice-capped mountains around him. It was only a matter of time before it
descended over the valley and forced Din to cover, making him abandon the trail that led to
you.

 

With a kick and a grunt, the Orbak under him began the steep descent into the valley below,
careful but sure-footed. Din shifted his weight as much as he could, being careful to prevent
the toddler tucked against his side from being jostled. Even so, the child whined at the jolty,
sudden movements of the descent, carefully bundled under Din's cape to keep him warm.

 

"It's alright." Din hoarsed, both to the infant and to himself. "We'll be fine."

 

Yet the words did little to assuage the gnawing dread within his thoughts. Much like the
distant, rumbling clouds the echoes of Din's mind seemed to reverberate with a taut
apprehension that had his muscles coiling against the biting wind. If the fury in his veins
threatened to burn him alive, the cold dread of your fate tempered it to a low crackle of dying
embers.

 

His thoughts drifted to you, imagining your cold form open and exposed to the elements,
trapped with a dangerous hunter that no doubt would turn you over to the Empire without
hesitation, who might even hurt you in the process. The thought of what wretched existence
awaited you at the hands of the Imperials made that insistent prickle of anger itched up his
spine, had him grasping the reins in a white-knuckle grip and his jaw clicking as he grit his
jaw harshly. Even so, Din forced himself to breathe through his nose, push that boiling fury
down into a low, simmering anger.

 

Instead, he turned his attention to the unsolved puzzle that was your abduction. It was a
mystery Din had yet to unravel, the reason why the Empire had been hunting you all this
time. It made sense that they were after the child, with his strange abilities to make creatures
far larger than himself float, of his enigmatic species and the secrets hidden within him. Yet
you, a simple mechanic from a backwater world who had unknowingly stowed away on a
random ship, now boasted a bounty almost as high as the child's.



 

There had to be a reason. Din had considered it before, pondered it over in his thoughts while
you rested within mere feet of him on the Razorcrest, had curled into sleep within the warm
embrace of his hold. Yet every time he mulled the question in his mind he had managed to
come up desperately empty-handed.

 

You had told him your story after all, and it had seemed like an honest one. It may have been
you decided to hide some truths about your past to him at the beginning, just for your own
safety. Yet after all the time you two had spent together, there seemed to be little reason for
you to omit circumstances in your past that would be cause for your bounty.

 

You wouldn't hide anything from him, and yet...

 

The image of your terrified face, of your voice crying out sharply in the darkness, of your
hands pushing him away in your terror clung to the edges of his mind like soot. It smeared
dark and thick against his fingertips, tarnishing the confidence Din had with your trust in
him. You were hiding something, you had been ever since that moment on Christophsis with
the Imperial Intelligence officer. Whatever it was had caught you so off guard, had terrified
you so greatly that you dared not even speak of it lest you summon whatever demons traipsed
the recesses of your mind.

 

Din had no doubt that whatever it was, whatever wraith had decided to make your shadow its
home, was the same reason you had been taken.

 

Yet the puzzle of your abduction posed only another enigma to him. It didn't make sense. If
the hunter had been nearby, surely they would have taken you back to their own ship before
fleeing the planet. Yet instead, Din had been told of an absent hover-cart from the village, and
of a suspicious bundle in the form of a person being loaded before the driver had vanished
into the early morning light. Whoever your captor was, they had decided to take you by land
to wherever their destination was.

 

The Orbak under him faltered on a loose stone, and for a moment Din had to cling to the
beast to keep himself from tumbling out of his saddle and down the mountainside. Yet
quickly the animal managed to right itself, chuffing nervously at the steep, perilous descent.

 



Din hazarded a look down into the valley below, visored gaze tracing over the misty trail
ahead. You couldn't be far now, not unless your captor had found another way to get down
the mountainside. Yet it was too far for Din to see properly, for him to make out any sign of
life on the path ahead. All he could manage was the village that sat at the far western corner
of the valley, lights glowing in the fog and snow whipped from the mountainside. He couldn't
make out any ships there as far as he could see, so it was unlikely your captor was trying to
transport you off planet. There was only a single road that bisected the town, winding through
before beginning to crawl up the opposite side of the valley where-

 

Din paused.

 

Gently steering his mount to a halt, Din fumbled for the scopes attached to his belt, eyes
locked on the smallest turn of the winding road on the other side of the valley. It took him a
moment to zoom in on what he was seeing, straining to find the miniscule ramp in the
distance through the ever-worsening storm.

 

A tower. A tower perched on the side of the mountain, partially obscured by the waves of
snow falling from the peaks. Din blinked, lips parting in concentration as he traced over the
steel gray outline of the building in contrast to the dark brown structures of the village it
overlooked. As Din continued to scan it became plain the other side of the valley was not as
desolate as he once thought. He could see it, could make out the outline of a bridge connected
to the tower, the frames and segments digging deep into the bedrock of the ridge.  sections of
it had fallen apart, collapsed into the mountain and had been buried under layers of snow, but
the frame remained. In it, Din finally began to understand exactly what he was looking at.

 

An outpost. One that had been abandoned for years, left after its previous owners had fled in
the wake of a new era. In the fall of an Empire.

 

The cold bite of the howling wind felt like a mere whisper to the realization that descended
onto Din's thoughts. For a moment he felt as if he had fallen off the cliffside itself, careening
and spiraling into the abyss below as he tried to grapple his way free of the panic and dread
that rose sharply up his throat.

 

An Imperial outpost. You were being taken to an Imperial outpost, one that might not be
abandoned after all.

 



 

 

 

 

Chapter End Notes

Din is beginning to figure out the truth, isn't he? It won't be much longer until all is
revealed, and both our survivor and Mandalorian are forced to confront each other's
identities, and their own. :3c
